title: Marketing of Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) lawsuits and social media misinformation campaigns' impact on PrEP uptake among gender and sexual minority individuals
screen_reason: Survey wave of a US national cohort (n=2,078) in which respondents were shown two real TDF/Truvada lawsuit ads — content the paper and a cited Lancet HIV commentary characterise as promoting false information about PrEP safety — and asked whether they had seen such ads on social media. 59.9% said yes: a self-reported exposure share with an explicit denominator (RECALL, exposure). All the paper's other numbers are attitude change or hypothetical behavioural intention and are excluded.

estimates.country: United States (all 50 states, Puerto Rico and Guam)
estimates.platform: Social media (ads described as appearing on platforms like Facebook and Instagram; exact source not collected)
estimates.date: Month-24 assessments from October 2019, data reported as of March 2020
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who reported having seen ads for TDF (Truvada) lawsuits on social media
estimates.value_raw: 59.9%; Table 1: Yes n=1,245, No n=745, I don't know n=88 of n=2,078
estimates.denominator: 2,078 HIV-negative cisgender men, transgender men and transgender women who have sex with men in the Together 5000 US national internet cohort who completed the month-24 assessment by March 2020 (2,204 responses minus 126 HIV-positive participants)
estimates.definition: Answered 'yes' to having seen ads like the two verbatim TDF lawsuit ads displayed in the survey ('Gilead TDF HIV Drugs Lawsuit…' and 'Warning: Kidney disease, bone loss or breaks, tooth loss and osteoporosis linked to Truvada…') on social media
estimates.misinfo_def: “A 2020 commentary in Lancet HIV noted that ‘these advertisements promote false information about the safety of PrEP [TDF] by suggesting that rare side-effects (e.g., renal failure and substantial bone loss) are commonplace.’”
estimates.source_quote: Overall, 59.9% of participants reported having seen TDF-related lawsuits on social media.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Exposure is a single self-reported yes/no item; nothing verified what respondents actually saw. The misinformation status of the ad class is asserted by the authors and rests on a cited Lancet HIV commentary and a Washington Post report — there is no coding procedure, coder count, or reliability statistic. The stimulus itself is fixed and verbatim (two real ads shown in the survey), which is stronger than the usual 'have you seen misinformation?' item.
estimates.moderator_quote: During their 24-month survey, participants were presented with two ads exactly as they appeared on social media. ... Participants were first asked if they had seen ads like these on social media (1 = yes, 0 = no).
estimates.notes: borderline=true flags a construct call, not a QUALITY/CONTENT ambiguity: whether plaintiff-recruitment legal advertising counts as 'misinformation' for this review. The case for including it — the paper's own title calls them 'misinformation campaigns', the cited Lancet HIV commentary calls them 'false information about the safety of PrEP', and the mechanism is misleading-by-emphasis (implying rare side effects are commonplace), hence breadth=misleading rather than false. The case against — the ad text quoted is not verifiably false, and the exposure item asks about seeing ADS, not about encountering misinformation. population_scope='other' because this is a high-HIV-risk sexual and gender minority cohort, not a general-population sample; sampling_frame='convenience' because enrolment was via ads on men-for-men geosocial networking apps (non-probability). Year coded 2019 (start of the month-24 wave); the wave spans Oct 2019–Mar 2020. platform_norm=multi_platform because the authors state they did not collect which platform ('Facebook versus other forms of social media').

missed_or_uncertain: (1) '27.7% reported that these ads would negatively impact their decisions to start PrEP' and '22.1% of participants reported that these ads would negatively impact their decision to stay on PrEP' — hypothetical behavioural intentions in response to a shown stimulus, explicitly excluded by the protocol. (2) '38.2% agreed or strongly agreed' with 'Ads like this make me think PrEP (Truvada) is not safe' (and 26.9% (strongly) disagreed) — an attitude/belief outcome, and belief in false claims is excluded. Likewise the within-group versions (27.8% of current PrEP users and 37.1% of past-year users agreed). (3) All demographic breakdowns of the 59.9% exposure figure in Table 1 (e.g. seen the ads: White 60.4%, Black 68.7%, Latinx 59.4%, other/multiple 50.6%; no PrEP history 53.2% vs current PrEP use 71.0%; meets PrEP criteria 60.7% vs not 49.4%; Northeast 62.2%, Midwest 61.7%, South 59.7%, West 58.5%) are demographic subgroups, not the paper's headline, so they are collapsed into the single 59.9% row per the protocol. (4) The 'I don't know' category (n=88, 4.2%) means the 59.9% is not simply the complement of a no/yes split — recorded in value_raw so the denominator handling is auditable. (5) No content analysis of the ads themselves was performed, so there is no CONTENT row: the paper never counts how many PrEP-related ads were misleading.

rob.design: Secondary analysis of one wave of Together 5000, an ongoing US national internet-based cohort. Enrolment Oct 2017–Jun 2018 via ads on men-for-men geosocial networking apps (non-probability); >8,000 individuals from all 50 states, Puerto Rico and Guam; eligibility required age 16–49, ≥2 male sex partners in past 3 months, not currently in an HIV vaccine/PrEP trial, not on PrEP at enrolment, HIV-negative, gender identity other than cisgender female, plus ≥1 HIV-risk criterion (recent STI, needle sharing, condomless anal sex, PEP use, or methamphetamine use). Month-24 invitations began Oct 2019; interim data to March 2020: 2,204 responses, 126 HIV-positive excluded, n=2,078. No response rate or invitation denominator reported for this wave; assessments were still ongoing, so the analysed set is an early, non-random slice of the cohort. All measures self-reported; single-item exposure measure with no verification or reliability statistic. Anti-fraud measures reported (US geolocation, single-use links, IP-address blocking, valid mailing addresses for HIV test kits). Authors' stated limits: self-report, hypothetical rather than actual behaviour change, no data on ad frequency or exact platform, no measure of overall social media use or trust, incomplete cohort coverage, insufficient power for transgender/non-binary participants.
